name: Sam Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A normal week is business and economics lectures Monday to Wednesday, then Thursday I'm usually flipping through listings for my resale side thing. I buy secondhand trainers and vintage jackets at car-boot sales, photograph them and list them online. Mum's a hairdresser who raised me alone, and she covers my rent share, but I pay for everything else. I use AI for everything I can: drafting listings, planning my week, explaining statistics I didn't follow in the lecture. My flatmates call me the guy who asks the chatbot first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, and it's still a useful tool. I'd tell my friends the people who said it would change everything were just selling something. Online I'd probably post a funny meme about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be a bit disappointed, because I find it exciting. But I'd be fine. If AI only does routine stuff, I already use it to save time on listings and that's enough. My degree still leads somewhere normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, and put more hours into the resale business, because that's where my money comes from. I'd try to move from forty listings a month to eighty and save the extra. I'd also apply for a summer job at the local marketing agency. I'd keep learning the new tools anyway, since it costs nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest. I like change, and a plateau is the opposite of that. But my money's steady, my course is fine, and I've got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. If it turns out to be mostly hype, what do you lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lose a bit of an edge. If everyone else stops using it, I'm no longer ahead of them. That edge is worth a bit, like knowing how to write a good prompt. But I don't need it to make my degree worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mum make of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum says whatever I choose, just don't end up in debt like her friends. She cuts hair six days a week and pays part of my rent from tips. She trusts me to be sensible. She'd actually prefer the plateau because it means nothing scary to worry about.

say: I'd say AI is still a **useful tool** and the hype was mostly people selling something.
Online I'd post a funny meme.
think: I'd be a little **disappointed** because I find it exciting.
I'm fine either way, since my degree and my **resale side money** don't depend on it.
do: Double my resale listings from forty to **eighty** a month.
Apply for a summer job at a local **marketing agency**.
Keep learning new AI tools, because it costs **nothing**.
feel: **Calm**, slightly bored, because my money and course are steady.
S0.quote: I'd tell my friends the people who said it would change everything were just selling something.
fieldNote: Calm because the **side income** and cheap rent cushion him, not because he ignores risk.
Disappointed rather than relieved: unusual for a first-year.
His mother's debt caution quietly shapes his habits.

steps.text: Raise resale listings from forty to eighty a month
Apply for a summer job at a local marketing agency
Try one new AI tool a month for listings and study

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment, and everyone should learn the tools, fast. I'd also say governments should make sure people who lose jobs get support. I'm not against regulation. I just want it to keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, business graduates are probably in the middle of it. Planning, reports, customer answers, all of it goes to software. But I'm one of the people who already knows how to use it, so I'd probably be OK. I'd worry for the ones who don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate more of the resale business, listing descriptions, pricing and replies, and go for a bigger market. I'd take the data analytics elective next term. I'd also look for a placement at a startup rather than a big firm, because small teams use AI harder. And I'd put money into an index fund from my resale profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, but a bit uneasy. It's a big change, and I like being on the right side of the shake-up, but I know it can turn on anyone, including me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you actually feel it, in the resale business or the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show them how, honestly. My flatmate Dani does all her essays slowly by hand and she's behind because of it. I'd tell her, use it as a draft partner and keep your own voice. But she'd resist, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your flatmates who don't use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The resale business would feel it first, in a good way, because AI does the boring bits. The degree would feel it later, when the courses start changing. I'd want lecturers to teach us how to use it properly rather than banning it.

say: I'd say this is the moment to **learn the tools**, and governments must support people who lose work.
I'm not against regulation; I want it to keep up.
think: Business graduates are **in the middle** of it, but I already know the tools.
I worry for the ones who **don't**.
do: Automate listing descriptions, pricing and replies in the **resale business**.
Take the **data analytics** elective next term.
Invest part of my resale profit in an **index fund**.
feel: **Excited** but uneasy, because it can turn on anyone, including me.
S1.quote: I like being on the right side of the shake-up, but I know it can turn on anyone, including me.
fieldNote: Sees himself as an **early adopter** who benefits, but admits the exposure.
Policy views follow his outlook: support for people who lose work, regulation that keeps pace.
Would teach flatmates rather than leave them behind.

steps.text: Automate listings, pricing and customer replies in my resale shop
Take the data analytics elective next term
Put ten percent of resale profit in an index fund
Apply for a placement at a small startup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge, and that all of us need to talk about how we share the benefits. I'd push for basic income and retraining funds. I'd say it in the student union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pretty scared, even though I use AI every day. If AI can do all the thinking work cheaper, then a business degree is a lot less useful. And I'd be graduating into a very strange job market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend most of my time on the side business, because it's something I own. I'd shift it to include AI-made designs and automated customer replies. I'd save everything I could, maybe two hundred pounds a month, in case I can't get a graduate job. I'd also join a local political campaign for basic income. And I'd probably still finish the degree, because it's only three years of my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, to be honest. Excited and anxious at the same time. I'd feel I'm at the front of a wave that could also crush me if I get it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is quick. What would you stop doing and what would you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on things I don't need, like the takeaways and festival tickets. I'd start doing market research on what people will still pay humans for. Things like experiences, trust, local services. If the machines do the thinking, people may pay more for real humans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change how you think about the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The degree might not lead where I thought. But the skills I learn, how to run a business and read the market, might still count. Robots coming three years later means shops and delivery might be safe for a bit, so I'd keep the option of working in those areas too.

say: I'd say this is **huge** and we need to talk about sharing the benefits.
I'd push for basic income and retraining funds, in the union and online.
think: If AI does all the thinking work, a **business degree** is much less useful.
I'd be pretty scared, even as an **everyday user**.
do: Put my time into the **side business** with AI-made designs and automated replies.
Save **two hundred pounds** a month in case no graduate job appears.
Join a local **basic income** campaign and still finish the degree.
feel: **Anxious** and excited at once, at the front of a wave that could also crush me.
S2.quote: If the machines do the thinking, people may pay more for real humans.
fieldNote: Excitement and fear sit side by side, reflecting an **adaptive** temperament.
Turns to ownership of his own business as the answer.
Keeps the degree as cheap insurance, not a bet.

steps.text: Add AI-made designs and automated replies to the resale shop
Save two hundred pounds a month for a jobless graduation
Cut takeaways and festival tickets to protect savings
Join the local basic income campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build a real plan, so go and do something. I'd tell my friends to get skills with AI and start something of their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I could get a graduate job at a startup and use it as a launchpad. Two years of experience while the thinking AI arrives would make me one of the people who knows how it works. That's a strong position, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with a good mark and get a first job in a small, fast-moving company. I'd put the resale business onto autopilot with AI and keep it going on the side. I'd save a few thousand and learn to code a bit. And I'd keep my eye out for a niche where human trust still matters, like advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. There's enough time to move, and that makes it feel more like a game I can play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, you'd graduate and have about two years of work first. What would you do with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the five-year picture I get a job, savings and experience first, which lets me be a player and not a victim. In the two-year picture I'm at a disadvantage because I'm still a student. That's the whole difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is it different from the two-year picture in how you feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be a bit worried about the last year or two, when full AGI hits and everyone's scrambling. But I'd have the side business and savings. And Mum could probably retire her feet a bit if I do well.

say: I'd say five years is enough to build a **real plan**, so go and do something.
I'd tell friends to learn AI skills and start their own thing.
think: A graduate job at a startup is a **launchpad** while thinking AI arrives.
Two years of experience would make me someone who knows how it **works**.
do: Finish the degree well and join a **small, fast-moving company**.
Run the resale business on **AI autopilot** on the side.
Save a few **thousand pounds** and learn some coding.
feel: **Uneasy** but not scared, since there's time and it feels like a game I can play.
S3.quote: In the five-year picture I get a job, savings and experience first, which lets me be a player and not a victim.
fieldNote: Time to work first is the key difference, and he sees it clearly.
Wants to **support his mother** if things go well, which adds quiet stakes.
Mood is uneasy, not calm, because he still names the last-year scramble.

steps.text: Land a first job at a small, fast-moving company
Run the resale shop on AI autopilot on the side
Save a few thousand pounds in the first job
Learn basic coding in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good thing to know, and it's time to build the support systems. Training, basic income, a fairer tax system. We can sort it out if we start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd privately be a bit excited. A decade lets me build a business, a career and maybe even a family before the big shift. I'd feel lucky to be young now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate, work a few years, and probably start a company in something people still need, like logistics or local services. I'd invest regularly, maybe a hundred a month. I'd take a masters if the job market says I should. And I'd keep using AI to move quicker than the competition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. It feels like standing at the bottom of a hill that has a long path up. I can see it, so I can plan it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. What would you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade lets me think like an investor, and I'd start the company earlier while there's still a gap where human founders can win. I'd also look at industries that robots reach last, like care and trades, and buy into them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who needs the most help in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People like Mum, who are hands-on but older. Hairdressers might have until 2039 or more, but then it'd hit them hard, with little savings. I'd want to look after her by then. That's my biggest personal motive for building something.

say: I'd say it's good to know, and now is the time to build **support systems**.
Training, basic income and a fairer tax system can be sorted if we start now.
think: A decade lets me build a business, a career and maybe a **family** before the big shift.
I'd feel **lucky** to be young now.
do: Graduate, work a few years, then start a **company** in logistics or local services.
Invest about a **hundred pounds** a month.
Look at industries that robots reach **last**, like care and trades.
feel: Mostly **calm**, like standing at the bottom of a hill with a long, visible path up.
S4.quote: A decade lets me think like an investor, and I'd start the company earlier while there's still a gap where human founders can win.
fieldNote: Ten years turns the whole picture into **opportunity**, consistent with his adaptive temperament.
His mother is his personal motive for building security.

steps.text: Start a small company in local services after a few years' work
Invest a hundred pounds a month in a global index fund
Look at trades and care for later investments
Support Mum with savings before her salon work ends

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most, because I'd be a student with almost nothing built. What would help is a proper cushion: basic income, retraining on a wage, and access to AI tools for people who can't afford them, like Mum's friends. If everyone had that, I'd feel much better about the whole thing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people my age aren't all scared. A lot of us are excited, but we also know it isn't evenly shared. I want to be good at this and also help people who aren't as lucky.

headlineQuote: I want to be good at this and also help people who aren't as lucky.
portrait: **Sam Nakamura** is 18, a first-year business and economics student, raised by a hairdresser mother who pays part of his rent.
He uses **AI daily** and runs a resale side business that gives him income and confidence.
He sees himself as an early adopter, with calm in a plateau and a ten-year warning.
His mood rises to **anxious** with a two-year AGI, though he says it is still excitement mixed with fear.
He supports basic income and regulation, and wants to build something that can also protect his mother.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario worries him most, because he would be a student with almost nothing built.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **cushion**: basic income, retraining on a wage and AI tools for people who can't afford them.
